According to a Reuters report, Apple has successfully defeated a proposed class-action lawsuit that accused the company of failing to prevent child sexual abuse material (CSAM) from being stored and shared through iCloud. Details are as follows.

Apple Protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act

According to Reuters, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise has dismissed a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in 2024, ruling that the case cannot be refiled. The lawsuit accused Apple of "failing to prevent child sexual abuse material from being disseminated through its iCloud data storage platform."

In the complaint, two abuse survivors, identified under the pseudonyms Amy and Jessica, alleged that images of their childhood abuse continue to circulate via iCloud, and that Apple deliberately refused to use existing tools to detect and report known child sexual abuse material.

The lawsuit specifically pointed to Apple's decision to abandon NeuralHash — a system announced by Apple in 2021, originally designed to match images uploaded to iCloud against a database of identified child abuse material.

Amy and Jessica sought to represent several thousand other survivors in the class action. Citing subsequent court documents, Reuters noted that the proposed class was estimated at 2,680 individuals, with "estimated potential damages that could reach as high as $32.8 billion."

They argued that the members of the proposed class were all affected by the same Apple policies and product decisions, and that consolidating their claims could reduce the burden and trauma of individual lawsuits. The complaint stated:

Returning to the court's dismissal ruling, Reuters noted that Judge Wise stated that "the lawsuit seeks to hold Apple liable for failing to remove or block user-generated content, which falls within the scope of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act." Section 230 is a federal law enacted in 1996.

In short, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act generally protects online service providers from being held legally liable as publishers for content created by their users. This provision has long been at the centre of debate over how much responsibility technology companies should bear for content shared on their platforms.

Reuters noted that although the case has been ruled unable to be refiled, "the plaintiffs' lead attorney, James Marsh, said they are considering an appeal and exploring other viable legal claims."
